claims.text: The initial Mg-containing alloy has a homogeneous, metastable solid-solution structure without pronounced segregation or intermetallic formation.
Service-relevant high-temperature oxidation or corrosion conditions trigger thermally activated Mg diffusion.
Thermally activated Mg diffusion leads to nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries.
Increased temperature raises Mg atomic mobility.
Mg undergoes segregative diffusion along grain boundaries.
Local strain gradients at grain boundaries promote intermetallic nucleation and growth.
Mg-rich intermetallic phases can form a continuous network at grain boundaries and interfaces.
A continuous intermetallic network reduces oxygen ingress.
Reduced oxygen ingress from a continuous intermetallic network retains or enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Discontinuous or unevenly coarsened intermetallic precipitates create local chemical heterogeneity.
Discontinuous or nonuniform intermetallic precipitates promote microgalvanic coupling.
Microgalvanic coupling associated with discontinuous intermetallics accelerates localized corrosion and lowers corrosion resistance.
The transformation is expected to initiate at service temperatures of at least 600 °C in oxidizing or corrosive environments.
Transformation kinetics are significantly slower in inert atmospheres.
Transformation kinetics are significantly slower below 600 °C.
Aging time and specific service conditions determine the observed microstructural evolution.
Oxidizing or corrosive aging at 600–800 °C is predicted to produce greater Mg segregation and intermetallic nucleation than otherwise identical inert-atmosphere aging.
Changes in intermetallic morphology are predicted to correlate with changes in corrosion or oxidation resistance.
